newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition vows loyalty, budget row goes on.
newsitem.headline: German coalition vows loyalty, budget row goes on.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's main political allies swore allegiance to his 14-year-old coalition on Monday while still stoking a budget row that is badly souring their relations.

Leading Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats made the soothing comments after a weekend of stinging FDP attacks on Finance Minister Theo Waigel, whose budget drafts they said were a mass of juggled figures that changed every week.

But the CDU, its Bavarian sister party CSU and the FDP also staked out tough stands in a row that could wear on for several weeks as Waigel struggles to draw up a 1997 budget within strict EU Maastricht treaty deficit-limit guidelines.

Kohl's powerful number two, Wolfgang Schaeuble, bluntly told the FDP to cut out the criticism and stop acting as if it hadn't known about Germany's budget problems until it had to agree this month to putting off a planned tax cut.
"There is no better alternative to this coalition so there's no reason to blame each other," Schaeuble, the CDU/CSU parliamentary leader, told German Radio on Monday.
"We were a bit annoyed they tried to dump everything on Finance Minister Waigel. We have to stop this feud and work together reasonably," he said in rejecting the FDP charges.

A shortfall of several billion marks (dollars) for the 1997 budget has opened up deep rifts between the CDU/CSU and the shaky FDP, which sees the crisis as a threat to the tax-cutting image on which it has staked its political survival.

The CDU/CSU, caught between a pledge to meet Maastricht budget criteria and fear of a backlash against radical spending cuts, wants to keep its budget options open and suspects the FDP wants to play tax-cutter at its expense.
The time for a decision is short. The parliament budget committee will meet on November 14 to work out the final draft of the 1997 budget before submitting it for approval.

Kohl's coalition, which on Thursday will set a new record as post-war Germany's longest-serving government, has only a razor-thin majority in parliament and currently trails the potential coalition of opposition Social Democrats and Greens in the opinion polls.
Waigel told his CSU party at its Munich headquarters that the government would survive until the 1998 election despite the FDP's threating comments about its possible collapse.
But party officials quoted him as saying he could not accept FDP demands for the "lawnmower method" of cutting a set percentage from each ministry's budget.
CSU secretary general Bernd Protzner stirred a hornet's nest by challenging the FDP to lead by example by cutting out popular subsidies in the Economics Ministry it heads.
While denying it wanted to gamble away the coalition, the FDP insisted it would block any tax increases to finance budget deficits and campaign for faster tax cuts than the CDU wanted.
"We have constructed a firewall against further tax hikes," FDP secretary general Guido Westerwelle declared defiantly.

He also insisted the hated 7.5 percent "solidarity tax" for eastern Germany, a levy Waigel could not roll back next year, should drop by two points in 1998. Schaeuble rejected this and urged the FDP to wait and see how the economy developed.

The arithmetic of Bonn politics shows the weak FDP has no alternative to the current coalition, unlike in 1982 when it had enough parliamentary seats to ditch SPD chancellor Helmut Schmidt's government and form a new alliance with Kohl.

But the FDP, which hovered near death until it survived three key state polls last March on a tax-cutting platform, could still slip under the five percent minimum vote in the 1998 election if it does not wrest more tax cuts from Kohl.
